articles.title: We Asked 20 Celebrities What Life Advice They Would Have Given to Their Younger Selves—And You’re Going to Want to Pay Attention
articles.content:
如果能与年轻时的自己对话五分钟，你会说些什么？停止过度担忧？信任自己的直觉？记得涂防晒霜？（真的，一定要涂防晒霜！）回顾过去总能让一切看起来清晰许多，无论取得多大成就，总有些教训希望能早点学到。名人也一样。

我们采访了娱乐界的一些大牌人物——包括奥斯卡提名者及艾美奖得主安杰拉·巴塞特（Angela Bassett）、两届奥斯卡得主罗伯特·德尼罗（Robert De Niro）、演员兼模特、畅销书作家布鲁克·希尔兹（Brooke Shields）——请他们分享给年轻时自己的建议。这些人对追逐梦想、冒险、应对挫折、以及在专业领域精益求精都有独到见解。他们的回答真诚、出人意料，而且非常真实可感。可以想象成是那些经历过风雨、如今希望能轻轻告诉年轻自我的一些珍贵建议。而幸运的是，他们选择了与我们大家分享这些智慧。

继续阅读这些成就卓著的明星们希望年轻时就知道的建议。或许你会找到自己需要听的那句话。

《 Reader's Digest 》的《阅读升级》新闻稿提供更多明星采访、名言、趣闻、幽默、清洁、旅行和科技等内容，全周精彩不断。

“要说的话就是，无所谓。我们纠结的大多数事情最终都没那么重要。你会发现，什么时候它们才是真正重要的事情，随着人生经历的积累。”

“我每天都会这样告诉自己，因为生活节奏太快。我也会这样对我的孩子说，他们总能接上后半句。我说，‘你不会跳舞。’他们会说，‘但每首歌你都能尝试。’”

“女孩，你要有耐心。要有耐心。相信我，一切都会如你所愿。唯一值得倾听并重视的人是你的父母，要善于判断。当合适的导师出现时，你会知道的。但你必须耐心一点，你这小急性子。”

“我对年轻时的自己有很多建议。记得我还是个孩子，可能当时十几岁的时候，遇到了一个商店的销售员，他说：‘要是年轻的时候就知道现在知道的这些就好了。’所以我有很多话想对年轻时的自己说。不过这并不意味着你不该去做某些事情，但要清楚后果。有些经历必须亲身经历才能真正学会。”

“要更喜欢自己。对自己更温柔一些。你不必总是答应别人。”

“不要在意别人怎么看你。为自己而活，而不是为任何人。”

“别理会噪音。安妮·兰伯特（Annie Lamott）有一个很好的概念，她称之为‘KFKD广播’。指的是那些干扰思绪的噪音。她建议降低这些噪音的音量，所以我会试着让年轻时的自己在脑海中降低‘KFKD广播’的音量。”

“别让不相干的人占据你的思绪。”

“继续做你该做的事。”

“记得涂防晒霜！”

“别那么担心。一切都会好起来的。你工作努力，别人看得见。所以没必要那么不自信。这已经在发生了。”

“我迫不及待地想让你知道接下来会发生什么。我会说，放松点，享受当下。”

“我会说，‘不’是你的朋友，不是敌人。我觉得这花了我很长时间，我现在四十多岁了，仍在学习如何习惯说‘不’。年轻时，我甘愿自己不舒服，只为了让别人舒服，这对自己不公平。学会说‘不’是一件很棒的事。”

“你做得很好。”

“继续前进。”

“我会告诉她，‘你已经很聪明、很美丽，你不需要伪装成任何人。你足够好。’”

“别听任何人，跟随自己的直觉。”

“忘记那些十几磅的体重——按你自己的方式去做。你会毁了新陈代谢，一辈子都会痛苦。算了。很快，你现在认为臀部太大的那部分，那种西西里风格的Kolie臀型，会变得非常流行，其他女孩还会想买这种臀型。所以别再嫌弃自己的臀部了。”

“我可能会告诉她，你做得很好，生活将会比你想象的更疯狂，所以别纠结小事。”

“只做你认为该做的事。成长过程中，我从未有过野心，更不用说导演或写作之类的。这些从未在我的意识中出现过。我只是追随自己的兴趣，但不确定这会带我去哪里。没有目标，只是想，我对什么感兴趣？然后沿着这条路走下去。”

在《 Reader's Digest 》，我们致力于通过领域专家和相关专业人士的协助，制作高质量的内容。我们依赖可靠的初级来源，包括政府机构、专业组织和学术机构，以及适当时我们作家的个人经历。我们核实所有事实和数据，用可信来源支持，并定期更新以确保准确性和及时性。了解我们的团队、我们的贡献者和我们的编辑政策。

articles.summary:
If you could sit down with your younger self for five minutes, what would you say? Stop worrying so much? Trust your gut? Wear sunscreen? (Seriously, wear the sunscreen.) Hindsight has a funny way of making everything look a whole lot clearer, and no matter how successful you become, there are always lessons you wish you’d learned a little sooner. Celebrities, as it turns out, are no exception.

We’ve interviewed some of the biggest names in entertainment—including Academy Award nominee and Emmy winner Angela Bassett, two-time Oscar winner Robert De Niro, and actress, model and bestselling author Brooke Shields—and asked them to share the advice they’d give their younger selves. And these are people who know a thing or two about dreaming big, taking risks, navigating setbacks and becoming seriously good at what they do. Their answers are honest, surprising and, above all, incredibly relatable. Think of it as a little hard-earned wisdom from people who’ve been there and now wish they could whisper it into their younger selves’ ears. Lucky for us, they’re sharing it with all of us instead.

Read on for the life advice these accomplished stars wish they’d known sooner. You just might find the words you need to hear.

Get Reader’s Digest’s Read Up newsletter for more celebrity interviews, quotes, fun facts, humor, cleaning, travel and tech all week long.

Eric Stonestreet

“I would say that it’s not that big of a deal. Most things that we get hung up on really turn out to be not that big of a deal. And you’ll know when they are [a big deal] as you move through life.”

Angela Bassett

“I give it to myself every day, because life is so hectic. I also give it to my kids, and they finish the phrase. I say, ‘You can’t dance.’ They say, ‘To every record.'”

Sheryl Lee Ralph

“Girl, be patient. Have patience. Trust me, it is all going to work out for you. The only people you really need to listen to and pay attention to are your parents, and use your sense of discernment. You will know those good mentors when they come along. But be patient, you little impatient person.”

Robert De Niro

“I have a lot of advice to give to my younger self. I remember I met a guy when I was a kid, maybe in my teens, and he was a salesman at a store and he said, ‘If I only knew then what I know now.’ So I have a lot to tell my younger self. Also, that doesn’t mean you shouldn’t do certain things, but be aware of the consequences. You have to learn through those experiences.”

Brooke Shields

“Like yourself more. Be kinder to yourself. And you don’t always have to say yes.”

Lance Bass

“Don’t care what people think of you. Live life for yourself and not for anyone else.”

Candice King

“Stop listening to the noise. Annie Lamott has this wonderful [concept], and she calls it Radio KFKD. It’s all the static and noise that can kind of cloud your brain. She talks about turning that noise down, so I would try to instill the concept of turning Radio KFKD down in my younger self’s brain.”

Neil Giraldo

“Don’t let people live inside your head that don’t belong there.”

Pat Benatar

 “Keep doing what you have to do.”

Michelle Monaghan

“Wear sunscreen!”

Alison Sweeney

“Don’t worry so much. It’s all going to work out. You work hard, and people see that. So maybe don’t be so insecure about it. It’s happening.”

Ted Danson

“I can’t wait for you to see what’s happening next for you. I’d say relax and enjoy.”

Adrienne Bailon-Houghton

“I would say, learn that ‘no’ is your friend and not your enemy. I think it took me a really long time, and I’m still in my 40s learning how to get comfortable with saying no. When I was younger, I was OK with feeling uncomfortable just to make other people feel comfortable, and that wasn’t fair to me. Learning how to say no has been a gift.”

Meghan Trainor

“You’re doing great.”

Russell Wilson

“Keep going.”

Aja King

“I would tell her, ‘You are so smart and so beautiful just as you are. You don’t have to pretend to be anything else for anyone. You are enough.'”

Debra Messing

“Don’t listen to anyone. Just follow your instincts.”

Lisa Ann Walter

“Forget about the 10 pounds—just be the way you’re supposed to be. You’re going to ruin your metabolism and be miserable for your whole life. Forget it. And it’s someday in the near future that big butt that you have, that Sicilian Koolie, is going to be so popular that girls are going to try to buy it. So stop hating your butt.”

Jordin Sparks

“I would probably tell her that she’s doing great and that life is going to be so insane, more than you ever dreamed of, and to not sweat the small stuff.”

Barry Levinson

“Just deal with whatever seems like the thing I should do. Growing up, I never had an ambition, certainly not to direct or write or any of that. It wasn’t even in my conscious mind whatsoever. I just sort of followed things that interested me, but not knowing where that was going to go. I had no goals set. I was just [thinking], What am I attracted to? And I just went down that road.”

We rely on reputable primary sources, including government and professional organizations and academic institutions as well as our writers’ personal experiences where appropriate. We verify all facts and data, back them with credible sourcing and revisit them over time to ensure they remain accurate and up to date. articles.title: Brace Yourself! You’re About to Get a Lot More Political Fundraising Emails Before the Midterms—Here’s Why and What to Do About It
articles.content:
In a democracy, elections are our collective voice—even if, in our specific democracy, the loudest voices seem to be a bunch of email marketers. That’s going to be especially apparent this midterm season, which is well underway ahead of the Nov. 3 election. Warm up that delete finger, because it will be getting a workout.
Why? Well, just when you thought your inbox couldn’t get any more stuffed with stuff you don’t want to read, a major email carrier recently launched new fundraising rules for political groups. And you can be certain they will take advantage of them. How much can possibly fit into our already-at-capacity inboxes? Just you wait. Things are about to get way worse—but there is something you can do about it. Read on for the details.
Get Reader’s Digest’s Read Up newsletter for more news, tech, humor, travel and fun facts all week long.
Google recently launched a new Gmail Verified Sender Program, which will allow “eligible, verified political committees” to send “policy-compliant and non-abusive messages” straight to your email inbox, bypassing the spam filter.
The program is open to candidates, political parties, political action committees (PACs) and similar groups registered with the Federal Election Commission (FEC) or other election authorities. To qualify, political senders must be verified, send emails from a public domain and keep spam below 0.3% of the total number of email they send. If users mark more than 0.3% as spam when the emails come in, senders can get suspended for seven days or booted from the program.
The policy went into effect on Sept. 8, so the new reality is well underway.
One reason Google may have decided to allow increased political fundraising is to reduce the number of lawsuits it’s had to respond to. The Republican National Committee (RNC) sued Google in 2022 for “throttling” its email messaging campaigns with its spam filters. The case was dismissed, but the RNC appealed. In January 2026, the RNC lost again.
Also in 2022, the RNC and the Republican Senate and Congressional campaign committees filed a joint complaint with the FEC over Google’s spam filters, which they accused of intentionally censoring their messages. The FEC dismissed the complaint. Other lawsuits and complaints over the years have met similar fates.
But back to the original question. Given the lack of a big announcement by the company, it’s not clear that Google does think it’s a good idea, at least in terms of pleasing Gmail recipients. Google quietly updated its Help Center website to reflect the policy change, underscoring the idea that it anticipates users will not be happy with the increased email traffic.
And this isn’t the first time Google tried this. Back in 2022, the company launched a pilot program that also prevented political emails from being filtered as spam. Comments to the FEC were uniformly negative, according to a review of hundreds of them by Axios.
The main one has less to do with the volume of spam and more with the senders themselves. Being verified under this program doesn’t tell you anything about the fundraisers’ business practices or where your money will go.
“I did a lot of work in Congress to crack down on scam PACs that send you fundraising,” Katie Porter, a former Democratic congresswoman from California, told CNN when the policy became public. “They say they’re going to help elect veterans, but when you look at where the money goes, 99.99% of the money goes back into the pockets of political consultants. This doesn’t do anything to tackle that.”
Another risk is scammers trying to mimic a legitimate political group to solicit funds, harvest your data or hack your accounts. In 2021, the Department of Justice (DOJ) charged three people with fraudulently soliciting $3.5 million from unsuspecting givers. And just before the 2024 election, the FBI warned of phishing scams, merchandise “no-shipment” scams and other fraudulent activity masked as legitimate political correspondence.
You can reduce them, but it’s unlikely you can stop them completely. Here are four options.

Why are we about to get an avalanche of political fundraising emails?

And this isn’t the first time Google tried this. Back in 2022, the company launched a pilot program that also prevented political emails from being filtered as spam. Comments to the FEC were uniformly negative, according to a review of hundreds of them by Axios.

Aside from an overflowing inbox, are there any other potential dangers?

The main one has less to do with the volume of spam and more with the senders themselves. Being verified under this program doesn’t tell you anything about the fundraisers’ business practices or where your money will go.

“I did a lot of work in Congress to crack down on scam PACs that send you fundraising,” Katie Porter, a former Democratic congresswoman from California, told CNN when the policy became public. “They say they’re going to help elect veterans, but when you look at where the money goes, 99.99% of the money goes back into the pockets of political consultants. And just before the 2024 election, the FBI warned of phishing scams, merchandise “no-shipment” scams and other fraudulent activity masked as legitimate political correspondence.

Is there any way to stop the deluge of emails?

You can reduce them, but it’s unlikely you can stop them completely. Here are four options.

  • Click unsubscribe. Google recommends that senders offer a one-click unsubscribe button, so use it. You can also open the message and navigate to the unsubscribe options at the company’s website.
  • Create a filter. In the search bar at the top, click the “show search options” icon to show filters. Or click the box next to an unwanted email, then hit the three dots menu and select “filter messages like these.”
  • Mark the email as spam. If a company does not unsubscribe you, mark the emails as spam. Know that this will not unsubscribe you, but it will send the emails automatically to your spam inbox.
  • Block the sender. If you want nothing else from the sender at all, open the email, hit the three dots “more” menu and select “Block [sender].”

articles.title: We Tried a Beginner’s Pottery Kit—And Now We Wanna Clay All Day
articles.content:
Time away from screens is absolutely essential, especially in the age of AI. That’s why the recent rise of analog hobbies has been nothing short of a miracle for my mental health. In fact, spending a few minutes with a mini coloring book or investing in a monthly book subscription is an easy way to boost dopamine during my downtime—no doomscrolling required.
But the best hobbies are those that require practice and patience. That’s where at-home pottery kit brand Pottd comes in. These clever at-home pottery kits come with almost everything you need to put together pots, paint mugs or make your bestie an incense burner. And the best part? You don’t need any experience with clay to craft cute pieces. Here’s my experience getting hooked on these all-inclusive kits.
Pinch pots, painted mugs and pressed clay coasters—oh, my! Pottd kits come with dozens of different projects that scratch that creative itch.
There are several kits on Pottd to choose from, which fall into two categories: painting and pottery. Painting kits come with premade items along with the paints to decorate them. Pottd offers dozens of kits that come with things like picture frames, mugs, beer glasses, coasters or vases—you name it.
The pottery kits bring additional choices. Pick from general creativity kits or opt for specific kits that cover things like biscuit-shaped coasters, candle holders, baby keepsakes, sculptural plants, games and more. There are also extras like molds and paints available à la carte.
I opted for a general kit with “retro” paint colors. Pack neatly inside the kit is nearly everything you’ll need to make several different pieces, including:
First, take everything out of the box and arrange it on a flat surface. Now is the perfect time to unfurl that junk mail or those local grocery mailers crowding in your mailbox—they make excellent protection for your table!
The Quick Start guide is a great resource when first setting up your pottery zone. It outlines any extras you might want that don’t come with your kit, such as additional tools. While I didn’t have a ruler or rolling pin on hand, I did take its advice to ensure I had a cup of water set up for smoothing and adding “slip” to the clay. I also grabbed a reusable paper towel to keep messes to a minimum.
Next, I highly recommend setting the mood. If you’re like me, that means adding some background noise and good, solid lighting. While you can absolutely make your pottery in silence, popping on a good podcast, audiobook, or your favorite album helps keep that creativity flowing.
The Quick Start guide also comes with several instruction cards covering projects like a trinket dish, pinch pot, incense burner, vase, draped dish, photo stand and plant pot. Reading through these cards is super helpful when you’re considering your first pieces!
For my first project, a pinch pot, I unpacked one of the clay packets and separated out 1/4 of the bag as instructed. The rest goes back into the sealed bag for future projects. I popped the instruction card into the cardboard holder and got started.
Overall, the instructions are detailed and perfect for newbies. They go over each step in an easy-to-follow format, leaving plenty of room for creative choices. I especially appreciated the continued reminders to use water and the included sponge to keep the clay surface nice and slick. This clay tends to crack when it’s dry, so keeping it moist while you work is crucial for a nice, smooth look.
After making my pinch pot, I caught the creativity bug and decided to crank out an incense burner and a draped dish. This time, I also had a clearer direction: I wanted to model them after my favorite noms—breakfast foods! Even after crafting a bacon-shaped incense burner, an egg-shaped dish and my little pinch pot, I still had about a third of my first bag of clay leftover. I didn’t even dip into my second bag, so each box can easily handle several projects.
The hardest part was waiting for the clay to dry, which took about 48 hours. After that, you must apply a base coat, which takes about 1-2 hours to dry. It’s important to ensure that pottery is completely dry before painting. Once dry, it was time to paint my pottery!
This is the fun part! Using the paints that come in the kit, it’s time to decorate your pottery. For the best results, Pottd recommends working in thin layers and waiting for each layer to dry before adding another. Now is the time to get creative with stripes, spots, murals or whatever inspires you.
I used a reference photo for my bacon incense burner, and I’m pretty pleased with how it turned out! While the kit didn’t come with a white paint for my egg whites, I opted for a baby blue color and think it turned out pretty darn cute. For my pot, I pursued a polka-dotted aesthetic.
Once the paint has dried completely, the final step is to give it a good glaze. This step is optional, but it gives the pottery a more finished look. Plus, the glaze protects the paint from scratches and adds slight water resistance, though it’s best to keep all pottery away from water for the best longevity. Skipping this step gives the pottery a more rustic look, should that be your preferred direction.
Once you begin making clay pieces from a Pottd kit, it’s quite an addictive hobby! I found myself thinking about my next project soon after finishing my first batch. And because each kit includes so much clay, I was able to make a few pieces to give to friends as gifts as well. Overall, Pottd kits are an easy way to try out a new hobby. I already have my eye on additional kits like the Paint a Tea Set kit and the overstuffed Super Bundle.
Pottd kits span tons of options, including pottery, picture holders and pretty tea sets!
Folks looking for an all-in-one kit that makes it easy to experiment will love how inclusive Pottd kits are. Plus, they make great gifts for creatives or date night activities for couples’ holidays like anniversaries and Valentine’s Day. The brand is always rolling out new kits and creative tools, so check out the Pottd website to see what’s currently trending!

  • 2 bags of eco-friendly Super Clay
  • 5 wooden sculpting tools
  • 1 potter’s sponge
  • 1 pottery paint set of your choice
  • 2 artist brushes
  • 1 bottle of base coat
  • 1 bottle of gloss varnish
  • Quick-start guide
  • An easel to prop up your guide as you work

Getting started

First, take everything out of the box and arrange it on a flat surface. Now is the perfect time to unfurl that junk mail or those local grocery mailers crowding in your mailbox—they make excellent protection for your table!

The Quick Start guide is a great resource when first setting up your pottery zone. It outlines any extras you might want that don’t come with your kit, such as additional tools. While I didn’t have a ruler or rolling pin on hand, I did take its advice to ensure I had a cup of water set up for smoothing and adding “slip” to the clay. I also grabbed a reusable paper towel to keep messes to a minimum.

Next, I highly recommend setting the mood. If you’re like me, that means adding some background noise and good, solid lighting. While you can absolutely make your pottery in silence, popping on a good podcast, audiobook, or your favorite album helps keep that creativity flowing.

The Quick Start guide also comes with several instruction cards covering projects like a trinket dish, pinch pot, incense burner, vase, draped dish, photo stand and plant pot. Reading through these cards is super helpful when you’re considering your first pieces!

Crafting the clay

For my first project, a pinch pot, I unpacked one of the clay packets and separated out 1/4 of the bag as instructed. The rest goes back into the sealed bag for future projects. I popped the instruction card into the cardboard holder and got started.

Overall, the instructions are detailed and perfect for newbies. They go over each step in an easy-to-follow format, leaving plenty of room for creative choices. I especially appreciated the continued reminders to use water and the included sponge to keep the clay surface nice and slick. This clay tends to crack when it’s dry, so keeping it moist while you work is crucial for a nice, smooth look.

After making my pinch pot, I caught the creativity bug and decided to crank out an incense burner and a draped dish. This time, I also had a clearer direction: I wanted to model them after my favorite noms—breakfast foods! Even after crafting a bacon-shaped incense burner, an egg-shaped dish and my little pinch pot, I still had about a third of my first bag of clay leftover. I didn’t even dip into my second bag, so each box can easily handle several projects.

The hardest part was waiting for the clay to dry, which took about 48 hours. After that, you must apply a base coat, which takes about 1-2 hours to dry. It’s important to ensure that pottery is completely dry before painting. Once dry, it was time to paint my pottery!

Painting party time!

This is the fun part! Using the paints that come in the kit, it’s time to decorate your pottery. For the best results, Pottd recommends working in thin layers and waiting for each layer to dry before adding another. Now is the time to get creative with stripes, spots, murals or whatever inspires you.

I used a reference photo for my bacon incense burner, and I’m pretty pleased with how it turned out! While the kit didn’t come with a white paint for my egg whites, I opted for a baby blue color and think it turned out pretty darn cute. For my pot, I pursued a polka-dotted aesthetic.

Once the paint has dried completely, the final step is to give it a good glaze. This step is optional, but it gives the pottery a more finished look. Plus, the glaze protects the paint from scratches and adds slight water resistance, though it’s best to keep all pottery away from water for the best longevity. Skipping this step gives the pottery a more rustic look, should that be your preferred direction.

Final thoughts

Once you begin making clay pieces from a Pottd kit, it’s quite an addictive hobby! I found myself thinking about my next project soon after finishing my first batch. And because each kit includes so much clay, I was able to make a few pieces to give to friends as gifts as well. Overall, Pottd kits are an easy way to try out a new hobby. I already have my eye on additional kits like the Paint a Tea Set kit and the overstuffed Super Bundle.

Where to buy

We Tried It

Pottd Pottery Kits

Pottd kits span tons of options, including pottery, picture holders and pretty tea sets!

Shop on Pottd

Folks looking for an all-in-one kit that makes it easy to experiment will love how inclusive Pottd kits are. Plus, they make great gifts for creatives or date night activities for couples’ holidays like anniversaries and Valentine’s Day. The brand is always rolling out new kits and creative tools, so check out the Pottd website to see what’s currently trending!

articles.title: Teens Are Getting Arrested After Posting a Dr. Seuss Meme—Here’s What’s Going On
articles.content:
随着网络快速发展，年轻一代的在线活动越来越难以跟上。虽然我作为一个90年代上网的老网民，对曾经的盗版音乐下载等问题了如指掌，但面对如今六七岁的孩子上网，我只能感叹时代变迁太快。近期，一个关于《喵喵猫》（Cat in the Hat）的恐怖梗图在网上疯传，看似荒诞却潜藏着真实的危害，甚至已导致多起未成年人被捕事件。

这个梗图最初源自2003年电影《喵喵猫》的黑色幽默片段，后来演变成AI生成的虚假恐怖内容，用户通过PS技术制造出《喵喵猫》在学校、社区或公共场所游荡的画面和视频。最早这些内容在8月份开始在Snapchat上流传，随后蔓延到TikTok和Instagram等平台，有时还配有恐怖音乐或威胁性文字。

"许多帖子声称这个角色将来到某个具体的城镇、学校或社区，以制造恐惧或暗示伤害"，德克萨斯州波特县警长办公室的斯蒂文·奥库特（Steven Orcutt）中尉解释道。例如，TikTok上有一条帖子写着："下一站肯塔基州，注意了。"一些梗图还涉及真实场景，角色被拍到追逐真人。

尽管这些内容没有实际暴力，但它们制造了混乱。奥库特警方表示："简言之，这是一场网络骗局，但反应可能导致现实问题。"例如，科罗拉多州格兰德朱诺克的14岁少年因发布涉及中学威胁的梗图被捕；堪萨斯州的15岁少年也因相同原因被拘留；密西西比州奥克斯福德的一个未成年人则面临与恐怖主义相关的指控。

更多州的未成年人也卷入其中。奥库特警方表示："我们正在调查一起与本辖区有关的未成年人案件。我们鼓励看到任何相关内容的人报警，以便我们能够及时调查潜在威胁。"

目前，这种趋势仍在上升，至少报告量在增加。"这些趋势将继续传播，直到下一个趋势出现"，奥库特警方说。换句话说，在下一个如"苏格拉底与骷髅"等病毒式梗图出现之前，我们还得面对这种人猫混合体的恐怖形象。

虽然没有真实的威胁，但这些画面可能会让年幼的学生感到不安，有时甚至会迅速传播，引发公众恐慌。此外，媒体报道有时会过度夸大趋势的影响。

这并不意味着我们不应该重视，但也要保持冷静。"当地报告的担忧主要集中在学生询问这些图像和地点是否真实"，奥库特警方说。

父母可以通过开放的对话来减少恐惧和预防事件升级，告诉孩子这些视频是伪造的，不是真实的，并鼓励他们向有关部门报告任何可疑帖子。此外，父母还应解释分享涉及学校和学生的虚假威胁可能带来的法律后果，"最重要的是，要参与到孩子的社交媒体使用监督中去"，奥库特警方补充道。
articles.summary:
At the risk of sounding old, it’s hard to keep up with what kids are doing online these days. Even uttering that sentence puts me firmly in the relic category, but … 6-7? Come on now! What are we even doing here?

The latest viral meme, involving a Dr. Seuss character who is definitely not teaching the youth their ABCs, seems silly and ridiculous at first glance—but is actually pretty terrifying. Sharing the meme has also had some very real, very scary consequences that you and your kids should be aware of.

I’ve been on the internet since the mid-1990s, so I have some big Gen X energy around online trends. My biggest fear was getting caught illegally downloading a few songs from Napster. (Which I barely did! I love copyright law!) But when I got a look at this creepy new meme, it had me wishing for the good old days.

To find out about this internet trend that’s increasingly getting the police called and has even led to some teen arrests, I spoke with Lt. Steven Orcutt with the Potter County Sheriff’s Department in Texas. Read on to learn what this viral trend is, why it’s a big deal and how to protect your children from consequences that could follow them around for life.

Get Reader’s Digest’s Read Up newsletter for more news, tech, cleaning, humor, travel and fun facts all week long.

What is the Dr. Seuss meme in question?

@cnn Videos showing a person dressed up as Cat in the Hat roaming streets after dark have spread across social media, even prompting responses from police in Ireland and the UK. But it remains unclear which, if any, of the sightings are real or if they are AI-generated. #catinthehat ♬ original sound – CNN

It’s called the Cat in the Hat meme. “This current trend began as a dark-humor meme using clips from the 2003 Cat in the Hat movie,” says Orcutt. “It has since evolved into an AI-generated hoax trend, where users create realistic-looking images and videos of the Cat in the Hat lurking around homes, neighborhoods, schools and other public spaces.”

The posts started on Snapchat and were circulating in Ireland and the U.K. in August, according to the Guardian. From there, they made their way across the ocean and to multiple platforms, including TikTok and, to a lesser degree, Instagram. The posts can be accompanied by creepy music and even threatening messages.

Why on earth is a Cat in the Hat meme such a problem?

“Many posts claim the character is ‘coming to’ a specific town, school or community in a way of inciting fear or making vague statements of harm,” Orcutt says. Case in point: “On my way to Kentucky next, be looking out,” read one Cat in the Hat message on TikTok. Sometimes the meme has a real-life element, and the character is filmed chasing actual people.

But no matter what form the meme takes, the idea is to sow fear and confusion. “While the trend is not tied to real-world violence, it creates several issues,” Orcutt says.

  • Unnecessary fear: Parents, students and the wider community are affected.
  • Wasted resources: “The fear creates false reports to schools or law enforcement, requiring resource-intensive responses,” Orcutt says.
  • Operational disruptions: “In turn, the reports create a disruption to school operations when posts reference specific campuses,” he explains.
  • Potential for escalation: The meme can lead people to mimic or exaggerate the trend for attention. “We’ve already seen that even a single alarming post can trigger copycat sharing or lead students to report concerns, similar to other online hoax trends seen in Amarillo,” Orcutt says.

“In short, it’s an internet hoax,” Orcutt says, “but the reaction to it can create real-world problems.”

Have kids actually been arrested for this?

Yes, several. “This is a national social media hoax, and not a localized threat,” Orcutt says. Teens from all over the country have been caught up in the hype and aftermath.

A 14-year-old in Grand Junction, Colorado, was arrested after posting a version of the meme that referenced a threat to a middle school. A 15-year-old Kansas kid was also detained over the meme, and in Oxford, Mississippi, a “juvenile” is facing terrorism-related charges over threats made to a “large school,” according to Mississippi’s WTVA.

Kids in Louisiana, Connecticut, Georgia and Texas have also been detained. “The Potter County Sheriff’s Office has processed one juvenile in relation to the investigation in our jurisdiction,” Orcutt says. “We, as an agency, encourage those who view anything of this nature to report it when seen and allow us the opportunity to properly investigate for any potential threats.”

How big of a problem is this?

For now, it’s continuing to rise—or at least, reports are on the rise. “These trends will continue to be shared, when seen, until the next wave of trends hit,” Orcutt says. In other words, until the next Socrates-and-skeletons viral meme surfaces, we’re stuck with creepy images of a life-sized human-cat hybrid.

“Although there is no real threat, the imagery can be unsettling, especially for younger students, and posts sometimes spread quickly enough to prompt public worry,” he adds. Be aware, too, that media reports have a tendency to elevate trends to larger-than-life proportions.

That doesn’t mean we shouldn’t take them seriously, but it’s important to keep the threats in perspective. “Locally, reported concerns seem to have been minimal and largely centered around students asking if the images and locations depicted are real,” Orcutt says.

What kind of conversations should you have with your kids about this?

“Parents can play a huge role in reducing the fear and preventing any potential escalation by simply talking openly with their children about hoax trends, reassuring kids that these videos are fabricated and not real, [and] asking their children to report any alarming posts to the proper authorities,” Orcutt says.

Also, parents should explain the potential legal consequences of sharing hoax threats involving schools and students, and “most importantly, be involved with their children by monitoring their social media usage,” he adds.

Sources:

  • Lt. Steven Orcutt, Potter County Sheriff’s Office; email interview, Sept. 15, 2026
  • Guardian: “U.S. schools and police warn about viral ‘Cat in the Hat’ trend after teens’ arrests”
  • WTVA: “Cat in the Hat AI trend leads to arrest”
  • City of Grand Junction, Colorado: “No Credible Threat Found in Social Media Incident; Arrest Made”
  • Connecticut Post: “Connecticut officials warn of ‘Cat in the Hat’ social media videos that threaten schools”

articles.title: This Is the Most Popular Cereal in Each State—Did Your Breakfast Favorite Make the List?
articles.content:
劳动节周末结束，夏天也随之成为回忆。这意味着开学季来了，当你匆匆送孩子去搭乘校车或拼车时，他们肚子里可能装着满满一碗麦片。

我妈妈禁止我们吃"糖麦片"（她的说法），所以每次有机会（通常在朋友家），我都会像在沙漠里饿了几周一样狂吃花生酱船长麦片。然后又回到玉米片——虽然现在我更倾向于选择含糖量更低的麦片。变老真有意思！

随着麦片季节再次拉开帷幕，我们想看看哪些麦片在美国各地最受欢迎。幸运的是，提供明尼苏达州圣保罗和俄勒冈州波特兰认证护理课程的CSP Global已经为我们完成了大部分工作。

接下来，我将带你一游他们的调查结果，这里充满了你童年时代吃过、现在仍然喜欢的麦片。继续阅读，了解这个早餐宠儿的知识。

订阅《读者文摘》的"Read Up"新闻通讯，获取更多关于食品、清洁、幽默、旅行、科技和有趣事实的资讯。

如今我们搜索很多信息，因此CSP Global没有从超市采集销售数据或打电话询问（谁会接听这些电话呢？），而是分析了谷歌趋势数据，了解美国人最想吃哪些麦片。

你可能会问，他们为什么这样做？因为CSP Global是一所护理学校，他们想了解州和地区趋势，并就营养和健康展开讨论。全国各地的麦片货架看起来大同小异，但当深入研究人们的搜索内容时，一些明显的趋势就浮出水面。

从这份名单可以看出，麦片界没有太大的变化。这些都是我们几十年来一直在吃的经典麦片。我的母亲肯定不会赞同其中大多数，但它们现在看起来确实让人垂涎欲滴。

以下是各州最受欢迎的麦片：

糖果圈麦片以13个州的胜利摘得麦片桂冠，是全国最受欢迎的麦片，且优势明显：这种热带水果风味的糖炸弹的最接近竞争对手玉米片和爆米花麦片，分别在5个州中胜出。

调查者还按地区分析了搜索数据，南部州使糖果圈麦片获得了压倒性的胜利。东北部和中西部（我的老家）更偏好基础谷物。阳光明媚的西部则更喜欢蜂蜜三谷燕麦片。

我心爱的明尼苏达州是唯一一个选择威铁麦片的州……现在想想，这并不太令人惊讶。1926年，明尼阿波利斯的一个广播电台播放了第一首麦片广告歌，而这首歌就是为威铁麦片制作的。

令人惊讶的是，小麦作为谷物在搜索中似乎并不受欢迎。葡萄干玉米片只赢得了一个州，缅因州，而糖霜小麦片也仅在怀俄明州脱颖而出。

另一个令人困惑的现象是：你上次吃苹果杰克麦片是什么时候？我甚至不知道它还在销售，但密西西比州很喜欢。最后，我家乡的邻邦爱荷华州是唯一一个选择船长麦片的州（但并非明显更好的花生酱版本）。有趣的是，我原以为他们会一心扑向爆米花麦片。

这篇文章原载于《读者文摘》。
articles.summary:
Labor Day weekend is over, and summer is in the rearview mirror for another year. You know what that means: school. And as you rush your kids out the door to the bus or carpool, it’s likely with a bowl of cereal in their bellies.

My mom didn’t let us have “sugar cereals,” as she called them, so whenever I got the chance (at a friend’s house, usually), I’d devour Peanut Butter Cap’n Crunch like I’d been starving in the desert for weeks. Then it was back to Cheerios—though I’ve moved on to cereals with even less sugar these days. Getting old is fun!

As cereal season gets underway for another year, we thought it would be fun to take a look at which cereals are the most popular around the country. And lucky for us, CSP Global, which offers accredited nursing programs in St. Paul, Minnesota, and Portland, Oregon, had already done the heavy lifting.

Ahead, I’ll take you state by state through their delicious survey results filled with cereals you remember as a kid and eat now as an adult. Read on to get a bowlful of knowledge about this breakfast favorite.

Get Reader’s Digest’s Read Up newsletter for more food news, cleaning, humor, travel, tech and fun facts all week long.

How did the report determine the most popular cereal in each state?

We do a lot of Googling these days, so instead of mining grocery stores for sales data or calling people on their phones (who answers those calls, anyway?), CSP Global analyzed Google Trends data to find out exactly which cereals Americans were hungry for.

Why did they do this, you might ask? Because they’re a nursing school, CSP Global wanted to get a sense of state and regional trends to start a conversation about nutrition and health. Cereal aisles across the country look pretty much the same, but when you really drill down on what people are searching for, some definite trends emerge.

What is the most popular cereal in each state?

When you take a look at this list, it’s apparent there’s not a lot of turnover in the cereal world. These are the same old classics we’ve been eating for decades. My mother would definitely not approve of most of them, but they sure sound delicious to me right about now.

Here are the most popular cereals in each state:

  • Alabama: Froot Loops
  • Alaska: Corn Pops
  • Arizona: Honey Bunches of Oats
  • Arkansas: Honeycomb
  • California: Honey Bunches of Oats
  • Colorado: Froot Loops
  • Connecticut: Cheerios
  • Delaware: Cinnamon Toast Crunch
  • Florida: Froot Loops
  • Georgia: Froot Loops
  • Hawaii: Cocoa Puffs
  • Idaho: Rice Krispies
  • Illinois: Cookie Crisp
  • Indiana: Golden Crisp
  • Iowa: Cap’n Crunch
  • Kansas: Trix
  • Kentucky: Froot Loops
  • Louisiana: Froot Loops
  • Maine: Raisin Bran
  • Maryland: Cinnamon Toast Crunch
  • Massachusetts: Trix
  • Michigan: Froot Loops
  • Minnesota: Wheaties
  • Mississippi: Apple Jacks
  • Missouri: Froot Loops
  • Montana: Rice Krispies
  • Nebraska: Lucky Charms
  • Nevada: Cocoa Pebbles
  • New Hampshire: Cheerios
  • New Jersey: Cookie Crisp
  • New Mexico: Honey Bunches of Oats
  • New York: Cheerios
  • North Carolina: Froot Loops
  • North Dakota: Special K
  • Ohio: Golden Crisp
  • Oklahoma: Froot Loops
  • Oregon: Froot Loops
  • Pennsylvania: Cheerios
  • Rhode Island: Fruity Pebbles
  • South Carolina: Cinnamon Toast Crunch
  • South Dakota: Rice Krispies
  • Tennessee: Cookie Crisp
  • Texas: Froot Loops
  • Utah: Rice Krispies
  • Vermont: Cheerios
  • Virginia: Froot Loops
  • Washington: Trix
  • Washington, D.C.: Trix
  • West Virginia: Corn Flakes
  • Wisconsin: Rice Krispies
  • Wyoming: Frosted Mini-Wheats

Which cereal earned the No. 1 spot in the most states?

Froot Loops took the cereal crown with wins in 13 states and was by far the most searched cereal in the entire country. And it wasn’t even close: The tropical-fruit-flavored sugar bomb’s closest competition, Cheerios (yes!) and Rice Krispies, each won only 5 states apiece.

What regional trends emerged?

The cereal analysts also broke out the searches regionally, and it looks like the South gave Froot Loops its dominating win. The Northeast and the Midwest (my old stomping ground) went for the basic grains. Out in the sunny West, Honey Bunches of Oats came in first.

  • Northeast: Cheerios
  • South: Froot Loops
  • West: Honey Bunches of Oats
  • Midwest: Rice Krispies

Were there any big surprises?

My beloved old home state of Minnesota was the only state to pick Wheaties … which actually isn’t too much of a surprise, now that I think of it. A Minneapolis radio station aired the very first cereal jingle in 1926, and it was for, yep, Wheaties.

What is surprising is that wheat, in general, turns out to be an unpopular cereal grain, at least as far as searches go. Raisin Bran won only one state, Maine, and Frosted Mini-Wheats also came out on top in a single state, Wyoming.

Here’s another head-scratcher: When is the last time you ate Apple Jacks? I didn’t even know it was still around, but Mississippi loves it. Finally, my old neighbor Iowa is the only state pulling for Cap’n Crunch (but not the clearly superior Peanut Butter version). Funny, I would have thought they’d be all-in for Corn Pops.

Sources:

  • CSP Global: “Every State’s Favorite Cereal”
  • University of Maryland: “Have you tried Wheaties? The Lost Art of Jingle Writing”
